title: STEM for Biological Low Dose Structure Imaging
content: Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) offers many advantages over fixed beam conventional transmission electron microscopy (CTEM), and STEM annular dark field (ADF) imaging and ptychography have become dominant in imaging of inorganic samples that are not greatly beam-sensitive [1]. For radiation-sensitive samples, however, a key parameter is dose efficiency: how much information is obtained per incident electron? On this criterion, phase contrast bright field (BF) imaging as done in CTEM typically wins over dark field techniques. One reason is that BF CTEM images are linear interference patterns between the unscattered and scattered electron beams, and for weak phase objects this is a more efficient process than dark field imaging (of squared amplitudes). Another reason is that a large portion of the scattered electrons ends up in the bright field (BF) disk and cannot contribute to the ADF image. This inefficiency grows worse as the resolution is improved by increasing the angular range of the incident beam.
